title: Test techniques: the three families
body:
# Why test techniques exist
A **test technique** helps you decide *what* to test (**test analysis**) and *how* to test it (**test design**). Instead of picking tests at random, you build a small but sufficient set of test cases in a systematic way.

Techniques help you to:
- define the **test conditions**
- identify the **coverage items**
- identify the **test data**

The syllabus sorts test techniques into three families. Section 4.5 then adds **collaboration-based approaches** (user stories, acceptance criteria, ATDD): a way of working together, not a fourth family.

# FL-4.1.1 (K2): the three families
**Black-box test techniques** (also called **specification-based**)
- Based on an analysis of the *specified behaviour* of the test object: requirements, user stories, the GDD.
- They do not refer to the internal structure.
- The test cases do not depend on how the software is implemented: if the code is rewritten and the required behaviour stays the same, the test cases are still useful.
- In §4.2: equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing, state transition testing.

**White-box test techniques** (also called **structure-based**)
- Based on an analysis of the test object's *internal structure and processing*: the code and its control flow.
- The test cases depend on how the software is designed, so they can only be created once the design or the implementation exists.
- In §4.3: statement testing and branch testing.

**Experience-based test techniques**
- Use the knowledge and experience of testers to design and implement tests.
- Their effectiveness depends heavily on the tester's skills.
- They can find defects that black-box and white-box techniques miss, so they *complement* them.
- In §4.4: error guessing, exploratory testing, checklist-based testing.

# One feature, three families
Take a crafting system:
- **Black-box:** from the recipe rules in the GDD, build a decision table of ingredient combinations.
- **White-box:** from the `CraftItem()` method, add tests until every branch has run.
- **Experience-based:** you know crafting often breaks when the inventory is almost full, so you craft with exactly one free slot left.

**Exam trap:** "black-box = you cannot see the code, white-box = you can". Close but not the exam idea: what matters is the **basis** of the tests. Specified behaviour = black-box; internal structure = white-box. A developer can design black-box tests, and a tester can design white-box tests.

**Exam trap:** "white-box test cases stay valid when the code is rewritten". The wrong way round: black-box test cases survive a rewrite that keeps the behaviour; white-box test cases depend on the implementation.

**Exam trap:** "experience-based testing = unplanned guessing". Wrong: it is a recognised family with named techniques, and two of them (fault attacks, session-based exploratory testing) are structured.

# Unity connections
- The weapon stat table in the GDD is a test basis for black-box techniques.
- A code coverage report on your Play Mode tests measures white-box coverage.
- "The last two releases broke saves after a language switch" is experience you can turn into tests.

# Side note for §4.5
Collaboration-based approaches reuse these techniques: an ATDD test for "squad name of 3 to 12 characters" is designed with BVA.

title: Equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis
body:
# Black-box techniques: the data ones
All four techniques of §4.2 start from the specification. This lesson covers the two that work on **data values**: equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis. The next lesson covers decision tables and state transitions.

# FL-4.2.1 (K3): equivalence partitioning
**Equivalence partitioning (EP)** divides data into **equivalence partitions**: groups of values that the test object is expected to **process the same way**. The idea: if one value from a partition reveals a defect, any other value from the same partition should reveal it too. So one value per partition is enough.

What can be partitioned: any data element of the test object, such as inputs, outputs, configuration items, internal values, time-related values and interface parameters.

Partitions can be continuous or discrete, ordered or unordered, finite or infinite. Two hard rules:
- partitions must **not overlap**
- no partition may be **empty**

# Valid and invalid: the spec decides
This is the part to drill. A partition is valid or invalid because of **what the specification says happens to its values**, not because the values look normal.

- **Valid partition:** values the test object should process, or whose processing the specification defines.
- **Invalid partition:** values the test object should ignore or reject, or for which the specification defines no processing.

Worked example: stamina regeneration. The spec says stamina is a whole number; 0–30 regenerates slowly, 31–70 at normal speed, 71–100 fast; any value outside 0–100 is rejected.
1. Valid partitions, one per *different processing*: 0–30, 31–70, 71–100.
2. Invalid partitions: below 0 **and** above 100.
3. Total: **5 partitions**, so 5 tests for full coverage, e.g. −10, 15, 50, 85 and 150.

The spec gives three different behaviours inside 0–100, so 0–100 is *not* one partition. Thinking only of the number range ("0–100 valid, the rest invalid") gives 3 partitions and misses two behaviours.

Second example: an ammo crate. The spec says picking it up adds 30 bullets; if the player's ammo is already full, the crate stays on the floor and shows "Full". "Ammo not full" and "ammo full" are both processed as the spec defines, so they are **two valid partitions**, even though one of them gives the player nothing.

**Exam trap (your logged one):** drawing the partitions from the number range alone. Wrong: the behaviours in the spec set the partitions.

**Exam trap (your logged one):** two partitions for a range. A range with values rejected on both sides has **three**: invalid below, valid, invalid above.

**Exam trap:** "the spec describes the error message for these values, so they are valid". No: values the test object should reject are in an invalid partition, error message or not.

# EP coverage
- **Coverage items:** the partitions, valid and invalid.
- **100% EP coverage:** every identified partition is exercised by at least one test, invalid ones included.
- **EP coverage** = partitions exercised ÷ partitions identified × 100%.

Stamina example: tests with 15, 50 and 150 exercise 3 of the 5 partitions = **60%**.

**Several inputs.** Many test objects have more than one set of partitions, one per input. The simplest criterion is **Each Choice coverage**: every partition from every set is exercised at least once; combinations are not considered. The minimum number of tests equals the size of the *largest* set.

Example: difficulty {Easy, Normal, Hard} and controller {Keyboard, Gamepad}. Each Choice needs **3** tests: (Easy, Keyboard), (Normal, Gamepad), (Hard, either one). All combinations would be 6, which Each Choice does not ask for.

# FL-4.2.2 (K3): boundary value analysis
**Boundary value analysis (BVA)** exercises the edges of partitions, because developers often get boundaries wrong: a boundary placed one value too high or too low, or left out.

- BVA works only on **ordered** partitions (numbers, lengths, dates), not on an unordered set such as character classes.
- The **boundary values** of a partition are its **minimum and maximum**.

**2-value BVA:** for each boundary value, two coverage items: the boundary value itself and its **closest neighbour in the adjacent partition**.

**3-value BVA:** for each boundary value, three coverage items: the boundary value and **both its neighbours**. It is more rigorous than 2-value BVA.

**BVA coverage** = coverage items exercised ÷ coverage items identified × 100%.

# Worked example: player level
Spec: the debug console's "set level" accepts whole numbers from 1 to 60; any other whole number is rejected.
1. Partitions: 0 and below (invalid), 1–60 (valid), 61 and above (invalid).
2. Boundary values: 1 and 60 for the valid partition; 0 and 61 for the invalid ones.
3. **2-value BVA:** 1 with its neighbour 0, and 60 with its neighbour 61 (0 and 61 bring nothing new): **0, 1, 60, 61**, 4 values.
4. **3-value BVA on the valid partition's boundary values (1 and 60):** 1 → 0, 1, 2; 60 → 59, 60, 61. Together **0, 1, 2, 59, 60, 61**, 6 values.
5. If 0 and 61 are analysed with 3-value BVA too, their outer neighbours −1 and 62 join: 8 values. Exam questions say which boundary values they mean: apply the rule to exactly those.

# Why 3-value BVA finds more
The rule "a stealth kill works when the enemy is 10 m away or closer" should be coded `if (distance <= 10)`, but the developer writes `if (distance == 10)`. With whole metres:
- 2-value BVA tests 10 (kill works with both versions) and 11 (no kill with both): the defect is missed.
- 3-value BVA adds 9: the correct code allows the kill, the faulty code does not. Found.

**Exam trap (your logged one):** answering an EP question with boundary values. For 1–60, EP needs one value per partition (e.g. −5, 30, 75); BVA picks the edges (0, 1, 60, 61).

**Exam trap:** taking both 2-value items from inside one partition (e.g. 1 and 2). The neighbour must come from the **adjacent** partition.

**Exam trap:** with decimals the neighbour is one **step** away: prices in cents give 9.99 and 10.00, not 9 and 10.

# Unity connections
- `[Range(0, 100)]` on a serialized field makes the Inspector clamp the value, so the invalid partitions cannot be entered there; scripts and edited save files still can.
- Stat thresholds in a ScriptableObject (0–30 / 31–70 / 71–100) are a partition table waiting to be tested.
- An inventory that holds 31 items instead of 30 (`<=` instead of `<`) is the classic BVA defect.

title: Decision tables and state transition testing
body:
# Black-box techniques: the logic ones
This lesson covers the other two black-box techniques of §4.2. Decision tables handle **combinations of conditions**; state transition testing handles **sequences of events**. Both are proven strong for you, so the questions use harder distractors.

# FL-4.2.3 (K3): decision table testing
Use **decision table testing** when a requirement says how **combinations of conditions** lead to different outcomes: business rules, loot rules, matchmaking rules.

- **Conditions** and **actions** are the rows.
- Each column is a **decision rule**: one unique combination of conditions, with its actions.
- **Limited-entry** table: all conditions and actions are Boolean (T/F).
- **Extended-entry** table: some conditions or actions take several values (ranges, partitions, discrete values).

Notation:
- **T / F**: the condition is true / false
- **–**: the condition's value does not matter for this rule
- **N/A**: the combination is infeasible
- **X**: the action happens; blank: it does not

Size: n Boolean conditions give 2 to the power n columns in the full table (3 → 8, 4 → 16). In an extended-entry table, multiply the numbers of values of the conditions.

Simplifying: delete the columns with **infeasible** combinations, and **merge** columns in which a condition does not change the outcome into one column with "–". (Minimisation algorithms are out of the syllabus scope.)

Coverage:
- **Coverage items:** the columns with **feasible** combinations of conditions.
- **100%:** every such column is exercised by a test.
- **Decision table coverage** = columns exercised ÷ feasible columns × 100%.

# Worked example: down but not out
The co-op GDD: a downed player with a revive token revives themselves. Without a token, a teammate within 5 m revives them. Otherwise they respawn at the last checkpoint.

| | R1 | R2 | R3 | R4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Has token | T | T | F | F |
| Teammate within 5 m | T | F | T | F |
| Self-revive | X | X | | |
| Teammate revive | | | X | |
| Checkpoint | | | | X |

R1 and R2 have the same action and differ only in the teammate condition, so they merge into one rule (token T, teammate –). The minimised table has 3 columns: **3 tests** for 100% coverage.

An infeasible combination: "level below 10" and "level 50 or above" can never both be true. Such columns are N/A and are not coverage items.

**Strengths:** the technique is systematic, so it finds combinations the requirement forgot (gaps) and rules that contradict each other. **Weakness:** the number of columns grows exponentially with the number of conditions, so with many conditions testers use a minimised table or a risk-based selection of rules.

**Exam trap:** "–" (does not matter) vs N/A (infeasible). A merged "–" column still needs a test, with either value; an N/A column needs none.

**Exam trap:** when the question gives a simplified table, count *its* columns, not 2 to the power n.

# FL-4.2.4 (K3): state transition testing
A **state transition diagram** models the behaviour of a test object as its **states** and the valid **transitions** between them.
- A transition is started by an **event**, which may be qualified by a **guard condition**.
- Transitions are instantaneous and may cause an **action**.
- Label syntax: `event [guard condition] / action`. Guard and action are left out when there is none.

A **state table** shows the same model as a grid: rows are states, columns are events (with their guard conditions), and each cell holds the target state and any action. Unlike the diagram, the table shows **invalid transitions** explicitly: they are the **empty cells**.

A test case is a **sequence of events** that causes a sequence of state changes (and actions). One test case usually covers several transitions.

# Three coverage criteria
1. **All states coverage.** Coverage items: the states. 100% when every state has been visited. Coverage = states visited ÷ states × 100%.
2. **Valid transitions coverage** (also **0-switch coverage**). Coverage items: the single valid transitions. 100% when every valid transition has been exercised. The most widely used criterion.
3. **All transitions coverage.** Coverage items: all transitions in the state table, valid and invalid. 100% when every valid transition has been exercised **and** every invalid one has been attempted. Test **only one invalid transition per test case**, to avoid **fault masking** (one defect hiding another). This should be the minimum for mission- and safety-critical software.

How they relate: full valid transitions coverage guarantees full all states coverage; full all transitions coverage guarantees both. All states coverage can usually be reached without exercising all transitions, so it is the weakest.

# Worked example: from the menu to game over
States: MainMenu (start), Loading, InGame, Paused, GameOver. Valid transitions:
1. MainMenu → Loading: `play`
2. Loading → InGame: `loaded`
3. InGame → Paused: `pause`
4. Paused → InGame: `resume`
5. Paused → MainMenu: `quit`
6. InGame → InGame: `die [lives left] / respawn`
7. InGame → GameOver: `die [no lives left]`
8. GameOver → MainMenu: `continue`

5 states, 8 valid transitions.

One test case, starting in MainMenu: play, loaded, pause, resume, die (lives left), pause, quit, play, loaded, die (no lives left), continue. Working: transitions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 3, 5, 1, 2, 7, 8. All 8 are exercised, so **one** test case gives 100% valid transitions coverage (and visits all 5 states).

A shorter test: play, loaded, pause, resume, die (no lives left). It visits all 5 states (100% all states coverage) but exercises only transitions 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7: 5 of 8 = **62.5%** valid transitions coverage.

Invalid transitions to attempt for all transitions coverage: `resume` in MainMenu, `pause` while Loading, and so on: every empty cell of the state table.

**Exam trap:** "every state visited = every transition tested". Wrong, as the 62.5% above shows.

**Exam trap:** a self-transition (InGame → InGame) is a valid transition and a coverage item of its own.

**Exam trap:** when every test case must end in a final state, a test case can reach only one of them. Count the transitions into final states before you count test cases.

# Unity connections
- An Animator Controller *is* a state transition diagram: states, transitions, parameters as guard conditions.
- Transitions from "Any State" multiply the valid transitions: count each one.
- Pressing pause during a loading screen is an invalid-transition test that finds real bugs.

title: White-box testing: statements and branches
body:
# White-box in one line
White-box techniques design tests from the **internal structure** of the test object. The syllabus covers two code-based ones: **statement testing** and **branch testing**.

# FL-4.3.1 (K2): statement testing and coverage
- **Coverage items:** the **executable statements**.
- Tests are designed to exercise statements until an acceptable level of coverage is reached.
- **Statement coverage** = statements exercised ÷ executable statements × 100%.

100% statement coverage means every executable statement has run at least once. So every statement that holds a defect has been executed, which may have caused a failure that shows the defect.

What it does **not** give you:
- **Data-dependent defects** can hide: `average = total / count` runs fine with count = 5 and fails only with count = 0.
- Not all decision logic is tested: an `if` without an `else` can be fully covered without its false outcome ever happening.

Worked example: five executable statements.
1. `if (hasShield)`
2. `damage = damage / 2;`
3. `hp = hp - damage;`
4. `if (hp <= 0)`
5. `Die();`

- Test A (shield on, the hit kills the player) runs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: **100% statement coverage with one test**.
- Test B alone (no shield, the player survives) runs 1, 3 and 4: 3 of 5 = **60%**.

# FL-4.3.2 (K2): branch testing and coverage
A **branch** is a transfer of control between two nodes of the **control flow graph**, which shows the possible orders in which statements are executed.
- **Unconditional** branch: straight-line code, from one statement to the next.
- **Conditional** branch: a decision outcome: the true or false outcome of an `if`, an outcome of a `switch`/`case`, or the decision to stay in or leave a loop.

- **Coverage items:** the branches.
- **Branch coverage** = branches exercised ÷ branches × 100%.
- 100% means every branch, unconditional and conditional, has been exercised.

Same code as above: Test A takes the true outcome of both `if`s, but the false outcomes (no halving, the player survives) never happen. Add Test B and both false outcomes run: **100% branch coverage with two tests**.

Branch testing also has a blind spot: a defect that shows only on one specific **path** through the code (one particular combination of branches) can still be missed.

**Subsumption:** any set of tests that achieves 100% branch coverage also achieves 100% statement coverage. Not the other way round: Test A alone has 100% statement coverage but not 100% branch coverage.

**Exam trap:** "100% statement coverage gives 100% branch coverage". The wrong way round.

**Exam trap:** "100% coverage means no defects are left". Coverage measures what ran, not whether it is right.

**Exam trap:** branch counts include the unconditional branches. When a question gives the number of branches, use it; for "minimum number of tests", work through the decision outcomes.

# FL-4.3.3 (K2): the value of white-box testing
- **Strength:** the whole software implementation is taken into account, so defects can be found even when the specification is **vague, outdated or incomplete**.
- **Weakness:** if a requirement was never implemented, white-box testing may not notice: there is no code to cover. Such **defects of omission** are found by tests based on the specification.
- White-box techniques can be used in **static testing**: dry runs of code that is not ready to execute yet, and reviews of **pseudocode** and other high-level or top-down logic that can be modelled as a control flow graph.
- Black-box testing alone gives **no measure of actual code coverage**. White-box coverage measures are **objective**, and they show where extra tests are needed, which raises confidence in the code.

Game example: the lag-compensation netcode has a two-year-old design doc that nobody updates. Coverage-driven tests on the actual code still find a rollback branch that no test ever reached. But a "spectator mode" promised in the GDD and never coded shows up in no coverage report.

# Unity connections
- Unity's Code Coverage package shows which lines your Edit Mode and Play Mode tests ran: statement-style coverage of your C#.
- A designer's pseudocode for an enemy decision tree can be dry-run with statement and branch thinking before any C# exists.

title: Experience-based test techniques
body:
# What the three have in common
**Experience-based test techniques** use the tester's knowledge and experience. They find defects other techniques miss, and their results depend heavily on who does them.

This section is on your extra-drilling list: learn the **exact names**. The exam puts invented names next to the real ones.

# FL-4.4.1 (K2): error guessing
**Error guessing** anticipates errors, defects and failures from the tester's knowledge, such as:
- how the application (or its earlier versions) has worked in the past
- the kinds of errors developers tend to make, and the defects they cause
- the kinds of failures that occurred in other, similar applications

Where errors, defects and failures typically sit:
- **input:** a correct input is not accepted; parameters wrong or missing
- **output:** wrong format, wrong result
- **logic:** missing cases, wrong operator
- **computation:** wrong operand, wrong calculation
- **interfaces:** parameter mismatch, incompatible types
- **data:** wrong initialisation, wrong type

**Fault attacks** are the **methodical** way to do error guessing. The tester creates or acquires a **list of possible errors, defects and failures**, then designs tests that identify the defects, expose them or cause the failures. The list can come from experience, from defect and failure data, or from common knowledge about why software fails.

Game example: your studio's last two titles shipped with an achievement that unlocked twice after a cloud-save sync. For the new game you add "achievement during cloud sync" to your attack list and design a test for it.

**Exam trap (your logged one):** invented names such as "error anticipation" or "defect prediction". The terms are **error guessing** and, for the methodical form, **fault attack**.

**Exam trap (your logged one):** calling a methodical, list-driven technique "exploratory". A **list of likely defects** driving the tests = fault attack.

# FL-4.4.2 (K2): exploratory testing
In **exploratory testing**, tests are **designed, executed and evaluated at the same time**, while the tester **learns** about the test object. It is used to learn more about the test object, to explore it more deeply with focused tests, and to create tests for areas not yet tested.

**Session-based testing** gives it structure:
- a **time-box** for the session
- a **test charter** with the **test objectives**; they can be treated as high-level test conditions
- **test session sheets** that record the steps followed and the discoveries made
- a **debriefing** afterwards, where the tester discusses the results with the stakeholders interested in them

Coverage items are identified and exercised during the session.

When it helps most:
- there are few or inadequate specifications
- there is significant time pressure on testing
- as a complement to more formal techniques

It is more effective when the tester is experienced, has domain knowledge and has strong analytical skills, curiosity and creativity. It can use other techniques inside a session, e.g. EP on a field you discover.

Game example: charter "Explore photo mode with extreme camera angles to find clipping and UI overlap, 45 minutes". You notice the UI disappears at 0.5× zoom, so you spend the next ten minutes around that zoom level: what you learn designs your next test.

**Exam trap (your logged one):** "exploratory testing is driven by instinct" or "random clicking". The exam idea is **learning**: design, execution and evaluation happen **simultaneously**.

**Exam trap:** "exploratory testing produces no documentation". Session-based testing has charters, session sheets and debriefings.

**Exam trap:** the term is **exploratory testing**, never "exploration testing".

# FL-4.4.3 (K2): checklist-based testing
In **checklist-based testing**, the tester designs, implements and executes tests to cover the **test conditions on a checklist**. Checklists are built from experience, from knowing what matters to the user, and from understanding why and how software fails.

A good checklist item:
- is often phrased as a **question**
- can be checked **separately and directly**
- may be about requirements, GUI properties, quality characteristics or other test conditions

Keep off the checklist:
- items that can be **checked automatically**
- items better suited as **entry or exit criteria**
- items that are **too general**

Checklists support both functional and non-functional testing (e.g. usability heuristics). They also age: items become less effective as developers learn to avoid those errors, and newly found high-severity defects call for new items. So **update them regularly, based on defect analysis**, without letting them grow too long.

When there are no detailed test cases, a checklist gives guidelines and some consistency. A **high-level** checklist leads to more variation between testers: potentially **greater coverage**, but **less repeatability**.

Game example, a controller-support checklist: "Can every menu be closed with the back button?" "Do the button prompts switch when a gamepad is connected mid-game?"

**Exam trap:** checklist-based *testing* (dynamic, here) vs checklist-based *reviewing* (static, §3.2). Same idea, different activity.

**Exam trap:** "all critical defects are closed" belongs in the exit criteria, not on a checklist.

# Unity connections
- A bug-database search for "after scene reload" is the start of a fault-attack list.
- One exploratory session per feature of each new vertical-slice build, each with its own charter.
- Platform certification requirements often become the team's checklist.

title: Collaboration-based test approaches
body:
# Testing together
**Collaboration-based approaches** bring testers, developers and business representatives together to write the user stories, their acceptance criteria and the tests. Their focus is on **avoiding** defects through collaboration and communication, not only on finding them.

# FL-4.5.1 (K2): writing user stories collaboratively
A **user story** describes a feature that is valuable to a user or purchaser of the system. It has three critical aspects (the **3 C's**):
- **Card:** the medium that holds the story, e.g. an index card or an entry on an electronic board
- **Conversation:** explains how the software will be used; documented or verbal
- **Confirmation:** the **acceptance criteria**

The most common format: "As a [role], I want [goal to be accomplished], so that I can [resulting business value for the role]", followed by the acceptance criteria.

Writing stories together, e.g. with **brainstorming** and **mind mapping**, gives the team a **shared vision** of what to deliver, from three perspectives: **business, development and testing**.

Good user stories are **INVEST**: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

If a stakeholder does not know how to test a story, the story may not be clear enough, it may not reflect something valuable to them, or they may simply need help with testing.

Example: "As a returning player, I want a recap when I load a save I have not played for over 30 days, so that I can remember where the story was."

**Exam trap:** the three aspects are **Card, Conversation, Confirmation**: not "Collaboration", not "Criteria".

**Exam trap:** the acceptance criteria are the **Confirmation**. They usually *come out of* the Conversation, but they are not the Conversation.

# FL-4.5.2 (K2): writing acceptance criteria
**Acceptance criteria** are the conditions an implementation of the story must meet to be accepted by stakeholders. From the testing side they are **test conditions** that tests should exercise.

They are used to:
- define the **scope** of the story
- reach **consensus** among the stakeholders
- describe both **positive and negative scenarios**
- serve as the **basis for acceptance testing** of the story
- allow accurate **planning and estimation**

The two most common formats:
- **Scenario-oriented**, e.g. the **Given/When/Then** format used in BDD: "Given a save last played 45 days ago, when the player loads it, then the recap plays before gameplay starts."
- **Rule-oriented**, e.g. a bullet-point verification list or a table mapping inputs to outputs: "The recap plays for saves older than 30 days. The recap can be skipped with one button."

A team may use another format, as long as the criteria are **well-defined and unambiguous**.

# FL-4.5.3 (K3): acceptance test-driven development
**ATDD** is a **test-first** approach: test cases are created **before** the user story is implemented, by team members with different perspectives (customers, developers, testers). They may be run manually or automated.

How it runs:
1. **Specification workshop:** the team analyses, discusses and writes the story and, if not done yet, its acceptance criteria. Incompleteness, ambiguities and defects in the story are resolved here.
2. **Creating the test cases**, by the whole team or by the tester alone, **based on the acceptance criteria**. They are examples of how the software should work, so "examples" and "tests" are often used interchangeably. Test techniques from §4.2 to §4.4 can be applied.
3. **The order:** first **positive** test cases (the expected path, no exceptions or errors), then **negative** test cases, finally test cases for **non-functional** quality characteristics (e.g. performance efficiency, usability).

Rules for the test cases:
- expressed so that **stakeholders understand** them: natural language with the necessary **preconditions**, the **inputs** and the **postconditions**
- they **cover all** the characteristics of the story and **do not go beyond** it (the acceptance criteria may detail issues the story describes)
- **no two test cases describe the same** characteristic

When the test cases are written in a format the team's test automation framework supports, developers can automate them by writing the supporting code while they implement the story. The acceptance tests then become **executable requirements**.

# Worked example: the recap story
Acceptance criteria: (1) the recap plays for a save last played more than 30 days ago; (2) no recap for a save last played 30 days ago or less; (3) the recap can be skipped with one button; (4) the recap starts within 2 seconds of loading.

Test cases, in ATDD order:
1. Positive: precondition: a save last played 45 days ago. Input: load it. Postcondition: the recap plays, then gameplay starts. (AC 1)
2. Positive: during the recap, press skip: gameplay starts at once. (AC 3)
3. Negative: load a save last played exactly 30 days ago: no recap. BVA adds the other side of the boundary: 31 days, recap. (AC 2)
4. Non-functional: the recap starts within 2 seconds of loading on the minimum-spec device. (AC 4)

Not an ATDD test for this story: "the recap can be shared on social media". It goes beyond the story.

**Exam trap:** ATDD vs BDD (§2.1). ATDD derives the tests from the story's **acceptance criteria**; BDD expresses the desired **behaviour** in Given/When/Then. The formats overlap; the input differs.

**Exam trap:** "ATDD tests are written by the testers after coding". Wrong twice: before implementation, and by people with different perspectives.

# Unity connections
- A story with Given/When/Then criteria can become a Play Mode test in the Unity Test Framework: an executable requirement.
- The specification workshop is the refinement meeting where the designer, a programmer and you agree on what "done" means.
